Prototype notes

Things to think with.

These experiments help you inspect a relationship or develop a possibility. Their value is in the questions they make easier to ask.

The commitment spiral

A deliberately simplified team model connects accepted work, delivery effort, delayed rework, fatigue and trust. Replay the same demand with different policies and intervention dates. Its numbers describe this model; they are not calibrated forecasts of a real organisation. The assumptions panel explains the mechanism so you can challenge the lesson it appears to suggest.

Explore the model →

Where flexibility gets trapped

A fictional battery day makes the interaction between state of charge, power limits and prior commitments visible. Offers and prices arrive progressively. Comparisons use the same scenario and information available at each decision. It omits many operational and market details; it is an optionality experiment, not a trading or asset valuation tool.

Play a battery day →

Reframing workbench

Different descriptions of the same situation make different actions seem reasonable. Develop several frames, state what they hide, then decide which intervention is worth testing. Example text is scaffolding you can replace. No AI evaluates your problem or decides which frame is correct.

Reframe a question →

Possibility mixer

A morphological thinking tool: define dimensions, combine their options, lock an interesting ingredient and vary the rest. The number of possible combinations says nothing about their usefulness. Capture a combination and explain what someone would actually do with it. That explanation turns a juxtaposition into a concept.

Mix some possibilities →

Your work and these prototypes

The tools run entirely in your browser. Saved work belongs to this browser and this address; another browser or the local copy has separate storage. Use the scaffold export buttons for durable copies or to move your work. Clearing browser data also clears local saves.

Examples are fictional and generic. The source is plain HTML, CSS and JavaScript with no runtime dependencies, external AI or data feeds. Each experiment is intentionally small enough to change after a real try.
